overview:
The state proclaimed in Bonn on 23 May 1949 was never meant to be permanent. Its founding document was called a Basic Law rather than a constitution, drafted over nine months by a Parliamentary Council chaired by Konrad Adenauer and approved by the three Western military governors, precisely so that it would not foreclose a future reunification with the Soviet zone. Yet the provisional arrangement hardened fast. Adenauer, elected chancellor that September, tied the new republic to the West with an insistence that overrode considerable domestic opposition: the European Coal and Steel Community, rearmament and NATO membership in 1955, reconciliation with France. The Saarland, held apart as a French protectorate, voted itself into the federation in 1957. Meanwhile the economy did something few had predicted in 1945, expanding through the 1950s at a pace that became known as the Wirtschaftswunder and made a bombed-out country one of the largest economies on earth. That growth ran short of workers, and from the 1955 recruitment agreement with Italy onward — followed by Spain, Greece, Turkey, Portugal and Yugoslavia — the Federal Republic imported labour on one-year contracts under a rotation principle that assumed the workers would leave. Many did not, and the assumption that they would shaped German immigration politics for decades.

The republic's second half was defined by two reckonings. One was with the Nazi past, which the Adenauer years had largely managed by not discussing it, and which the student movement of the late 1960s forced open with a bluntness that split families as much as parties. The other was with the division itself. Willy Brandt, chancellor from 1969, abandoned the doctrine of refusing relations with any state that recognised East Berlin, and pursued treaties with Moscow, Warsaw and finally East Berlin that traded formal acceptance of postwar borders for practical contact across them. Ostpolitik won Brandt a Nobel Peace Prize and bitter accusations of betrayal at home. The 1970s then brought the oil shocks, the recruitment stop of November 1973, and the murders and kidnappings of the Red Army Faction, which tested how far a democracy conscious of its own history would go in defending itself.

Helmut Kohl, chancellor from 1982, was governing a settled and unspectacular country when the East German regime collapsed in the autumn of 1989. Reunification followed with startling speed, and it took a specific legal form: not the drafting of a new all-German constitution, but the accession of five reconstituted eastern states and Berlin to the existing Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The Basic Law stayed, the Bundestag became an all-German parliament that December, and parliament soon voted to move itself from Bonn to Berlin. The provisional republic had outlasted the state it was provisional against, and then absorbed it.
significance: West Germany is the strongest modern case for the proposition that a democracy can be built deliberately, out of the wreckage of the regime that destroyed the last one, and that it can hold. The Basic Law's design — federalism, a constitutional court with real teeth, a chancellor removable only by electing a successor, basic rights placed beyond amendment — was a point-by-point response to how Weimar had failed, and it worked well enough that reunified Germany simply kept it. Its Western integration reversed a century of Franco-German enmity and supplied the anchor around which the European Union grew; its social market economy became an exportable model; its long, painful public argument over how a nation confronts its own crimes became a reference point for societies facing the same question elsewhere. And its guest worker programme, designed on the false premise that labour migration is temporary, turned Germany into a country of immigration that spent thirty years denying it was one.
coverage: Written from general reference works and institutional overviews from the Bundestag and a German migration museum; the dataset itself holds no events for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date beyond what the narrative supplies. West Germany is exceptionally well documented — open archives, a free press, an enormous scholarly literature — but this summary is a compression of forty-one years and skips almost everything: the Berlin question and the city's anomalous legal status, the 1968 emergency laws, environmental politics and the rise of the Greens, the Historikerstreit, and the internal debates over the terms of unification, which were contested at the time and remain so.
